## Libertarianism and Human Nature: The Adoption Problem
URL: /theses/2026-06-08-libertarianism-and-the-adoption-problem
Category: thesis

# Libertarianism and Human Nature: The Adoption Problem

> A hard version of the reader's puzzle is tested against the corpus: libertarianism may be internally correct, but given total payment surveillance, AI analysis, the military and treaty apparatus of nation-states, and a propaganda advantage that dwarfs libertarian education, can any set of free individuals coordinate into something the state does not crush? The reader's own intuition is that liberty could win only through an economic apocalypse no one wants, or through a new unifying idea — perhaps a creed with liberty at its core. The corpus largely concedes the diagnosis and gives a narrower, grimmer answer than triumphalism allows.

## The Claim Being Tested

The reader's challenge, restated in their own terms (this is the proposition under test, not a quotation from a source):

> *Libertarianism is correct and consistent but hard to adopt and sect-ridden, while nationalism unites millions. Worse: given today's surveillance, AI, and military states, free individuals cannot coordinate beyond the reach of nation-states, and libertarian education is out-gunned by mass schooling and big-media propaganda. So liberty could succeed only through an economic apocalypse, or through a new unifying discourse — e.g. a religion with libertarianism at its core.*

## Verdict in Brief

On the facts, the corpus agrees almost completely, and is candid that the obstacle is the terrain, not the argument: obedience runs on habit, legitimacy is manufactured, the opinion battle is structurally lopsided, and tribal sentiment gives nationalism a standing head start. The classic libertarian answers — withdrawal, the contest of opinion, and exit — are each **necessary but, on their own, insufficient** against the modern asymmetry the reader describes. What the corpus offers instead of optimism is a narrowing: **one hard floor** (the cryptographic cost-asymmetry, the single lever that does not scale with the adversary's size or AI), **one catalyst worth pre-positioning for** (a *monetary* reckoning, distinct from the war-or-emergency collapse that history shows ratchets state power), and **one thing the movement has not built** — the unifying meaning the reader rightly says it needs. The reader's two intuitions are not outside the tradition; they are its frontier.

## Why Adoption Is Hard

The oldest answer in the corpus is that obedience is habituated, not compelled. [[the-politics-of-obedience|The Politics of Obedience]] holds that a tiny ruling minority dominates a vast population through custom, dependence, and withdrawn resistance, so that subjection becomes second nature. Liberty is hard in a specific way: it asks people to un-learn a habit, not merely weigh an argument.

The habit is reinforced from above, and this is where the reader's propaganda point lands hardest. [[state-power-and-intervention|State Power and Intervention]], via [[murray-n-rothbard|Rothbard]], holds that the state's long-run problem is ideological, and that manufacturing consent is the work of intellectuals:

> For the masses of men do not create their own ideas, or indeed think through these ideas independently; they follow passively the ideas adopted and disseminated by the body of intellectuals.
>
> — [[murray-n-rothbard|Murray Rothbard]], [[anatomy-of-the-state|Anatomy of the State]]

With schools, mass media, and the prestige economy oriented toward the legitimacy of the "we," the reader is right that libertarian education starts several lengths behind — a point the corpus concedes rather than rebuts.

And where opinion could be contested, the ballot box is rigged by structure. [[public-choice-and-rational-ignorance|Public Choice and Rational Ignorance]] gives the demand-side reason:

> "Voter ignorance is rational because the cost of gathering information about an upcoming election is high relative to the benefits of voting."
>
> — [[william-f-shughart-ii|William F. Shughart II]], “Public Choice” (Concise Encyclopedia of Economics)

The supply-side reason is structural too: intervention accretes regardless of who wins, because small concentrated interests out-organize the diffuse public. Liberty is a systematically under-supplied good.

## Why Nationalism Is Easy

The asymmetry is not a marketing accident: nationalism has its raw material, its builder, and its market all working in concert. The raw material is tribal and needs no teaching — Sumner's ethnocentrism:

> "Each group nourishes its own pride and vanity, boasts itself superior, exalts its own divinities, and looks with contempt on outsiders."
>
> — [[william-graham-sumner|William Graham Sumner]], [[folkways|Folkways]]

The state refines that sentiment into national identity as part of its own consolidation, manufacturing it through direct rule and military mobilization, so that the loyalty it needs is produced by the very process that builds it. And it lands on fertile ground, because atomized, interchangeable people are starved for exactly what it offers — belonging, an enemy, and certainty in a single package — and so are available to be mobilized *en masse*. Each of these legs is documented in the corpus: the tribal raw material in [[in-group-out-group-tribalism|In-Group/Out-Group Tribalism]], the state-making channel in [[nationalism-and-state-formation|Nationalism and State Formation]] via [[charles-tilly|Tilly]], and the lonely-mass demand in [[mass-society-and-atomization|Mass Society and Atomization]] via [[hannah-arendt|Arendt]]. Nationalism is easy because the state paves its road and the lonely psyche craves what it sells — neither of which bears on whether it is *true*. This is the standing edge the reader names, and the corpus does not dispute it.

## The Internal Sects Are Real — But Share a Spine

The reader is right that libertarianism is sect-ridden. [[rothbard-vs-hayek|Rothbard vs. Hayek]] charts the fault lines — praxeology vs. evolutionary empiricism, calculation vs. knowledge, anarcho-capitalism vs. limited government — and [[mises-and-hayek-dehomogenized|Salerno's dehomogenization thesis]] argues that the Misesian and Hayekian lines are two paradigms rather than one reading of a single doctrine — a Mises/Hayek contrast, not a Rothbard/Hayek one, so the sect split above is this wiki's application of that map rather than Salerno's own classification. But the same articles mark the limit: the schools share a property-and-exchange spine and divide over method, the role of the state, and moral grounding. They divide over the coercion test too, and it is worth not softening that: in [[the-ethics-of-liberty|The Ethics of Liberty]] Ch. 28 Rothbard calls Hayek's definition of coercion "the fundamental and grievous flaw in Hayek's system", because it reaches "peaceful and non-aggressive actions as well" rather than only the invasive use of force. What survives is narrower than a shared test: a shared subject matter. The orthodoxies raise the cost of entry; they are not evidence of incoherence. (They also bear on the reader's "creed" intuition below: a movement that argues this much internally is poorly shaped to become a unifying faith.)

## The Three Classic Routes — Each Necessary, None Sufficient

The corpus's first instinct is to route around the mass-belonging contest rather than win it. Three strategies recur, and the honest reading is that each is necessary but cannot carry the load alone.

First, **withdrawal**. If domination rests on habitual cooperation, it dissolves when that cooperation is withdrawn. La Boétie's [[the-politics-of-obedience|The Politics of Obedience]] compresses it:

> Resolve to serve no more, and you are at once freed.
>
> — [[etienne-de-la-boetie|Étienne de la Boétie]], [[the-politics-of-obedience|The Discourse of Voluntary Servitude]]

Necessary, but slow and reversible, and it presumes a critical mass willing to stop cooperating.

Second, **the contest of opinion**. [[for-a-new-liberty|For a New Liberty]] treats education and ideas as the decisive front. This is the **weakest leg**, and the reader's objection is decisive against it taken alone: against statized schooling and mass media, an education strategy is structurally out-gunned. It can shift the margin; it cannot win the center.

Third, **exit** — the strongest of the three. [[agorism-and-counter-economics|Agorism and Counter-Economics]] proposes growing the counter-economy until it displaces the state, explicitly with *"no change in human nature needed"* — the precise answer to the coordination worry, since it needs participation, not mass conversion. [[parallel-economy|The Parallel Economy]] updates it with a cryptographic stack that aims to make coercion *uneconomic*. But exit collides head-on with the reader's surveillance objection, which the next section takes seriously.

## The Surveillance Asymmetry and the Cryptographic Wager

The reader's sharpest point: total payment tracking, AI analysis, and CBDCs make the state's observation so cheap and complete that exit is futile. The corpus takes this seriously rather than dismissing it. Its sharpest statement is [[max-hillebrand|Hillebrand]]'s critique of central-bank digital currency as *total intervention* — [[hillebrand-on-cbdcs|Hillebrand on CBDCs]] — that CBDCs are programmable money enabling comprehensive surveillance and control, not simple digital versions of existing currency.

That is a contested argument, not a settled fact. Hillebrand supplies the reason it is contestable — but he offers it as an indictment, not as a concession, and the sentences that follow are the sharp end of it:

> "Programmability is a design choice, not an inherent feature of digital currency. A CBDC could be designed to replicate cash's properties: anonymous, bearer-based, and free of spending restrictions. That central banks consistently choose surveillance-enabling designs reflects institutional incentives, not technical necessity. The designs being deployed and piloted reveal the intended use."
>
> — [[max-hillebrand|Max Hillebrand]], [[the-praxeology-of-privacy|The Praxeology of Privacy]]

The issuers of the leading CBDC projects say theirs will be just that — cash-like, intermediated through private providers rather than direct central-bank accounts, and never programmed to restrict spending — and the critique's reply is not that they are lying but that each of these is a policy commitment, revocable by the same authority that made it, rather than a technical guarantee. The thesis does not need the strong version of the claim, and the CBDC dispute can be set aside entirely. Even granting every design promise, the uncontested trend is enough: exposed digital payment is increasingly cheap to observe, and AI sharpens the analysis of whatever is exposed. The whole counter then rests on one lever — the [[resistance-axiom|resistance axiom]]: the claim that **cryptography is the one asymmetry that does not scale with the adversary's size or intelligence.** A sound key is as unbreakable for a superpower with the best models as for anyone; AI analyzes data that is *exposed*, it does not break good cryptography. The strategy is therefore not to out-surveil the state — impossible, as the reader says — but to make activity *unobservable in the first place*, breaking the loop at observation. When observation becomes expensive enough, the entire attack cycle becomes uneconomical.

The strategic payoff, in [[parallel-economy|the parallel economy]], is blunt: *"The state cannot persist when theft becomes unprofitable."* This is the corpus's one hard floor under the reader's pessimism — and the honesty is that it is a **wager, not a proof**. The [[resistance-axiom|resistance axiom]] is, in its own statement, weaker than a self-evident truth: a working assumption backed by computational hardness and the operational survival of Bitcoin, Tor, and PGP, defeatable by physical coercion, developer prosecution, key mistakes, or centralization. Whether mathematics holds the line against a determined state is the open question on which the whole strategy turns.

## Which Collapse? The War-Ratchet vs. the Monetary Reckoning

The reader's "economic apocalypse" intuition is half-right, and the corpus splits it on a distinction that is the whole game. Not every collapse runs one way — the Soviet dissolution in 1991 destroyed a state outright rather than strengthening it — but the *crisis* kind the reader has in mind, war and emergency, carries a documented ratchet toward state power. Rothbard states it:

> In war, State power is pushed to its ultimate, and, under the slogans of "defense" and "emergency," it can impose a tyranny upon the public such as might be openly resisted in time of peace.
>
> — [[murray-n-rothbard|Murray Rothbard]], [[anatomy-of-the-state|Anatomy of the State]]

Arendt's [[mass-society-and-atomization|mass-society]] account agrees from the other side: crisis-driven atomization feeds mobilization, not freedom. The Depression produced the New Deal and fed the Nazis' rise to power; war breeds permanent state growth. The *emergency* kind of apocalypse tends to birth a worse Leviathan, not a freer order — which is the gamble the reader's intuition quietly runs.

But a *monetary* reckoning is the one crisis the corpus reads as potentially pro-liberty, because it strikes at the state's money itself — not its largest revenue line (taxation is far bigger) but its most covert one, the inflation lever that funds spending without a vote and that it can least openly defend. The fiat-endgame thread — [[fiat-as-engineered-system|Fiat as Engineered System]], Austrian business-cycle theory, and the [[hard-money|hard money]] / [[ideal-money|ideal money]] lineage — holds that discretionary fiat is unsustainable, that inflation is a covert, non-consensual transfer, and that its eventual failure discredits the state's money. Read alongside *Anatomy*'s point that the state is the one organization that funds itself by coercion rather than voluntary payment, the printing press is simply the quietest of those coercions — and a sound-money reckoning is the one event that takes that quiet lever away. The decisive condition is that this opens a door **only if the hard-money lifeboat is already built and adopted** when the reckoning comes. That reframes the reader's apocalypse: the point is not to wish for collapse, but to pre-position the alternative — which is exactly why the exit infrastructure matters before, not after.

## The Unifying-Creed Problem

The reader's deepest intuition — that liberty may need a new unifying discourse, even a creed — is the one the published thesis underweighted, and the corpus quietly supports it. Domination, on La Boétie's account, runs on shared belief and withdrawn consent; Arendt and Sumner show that what mobilizes is *belonging*, not argument. You do not beat a legitimating myth with a syllogism; you beat it by withdrawing consent **and** supplying an alternative shared meaning. Where the corpus gestures at candidates it does so through its own articles, not the sources cited for this thesis — and none is shown to rival nationalism's reach. The wiki's article on [[objectivism|Objectivism]] describes a philosophy deliberately organized as a movement with liberty at its core; its [[cypherpunk|cypherpunk]] topic describes a culture organized around founding manifestos and shared practices; and [[hans-hermann-hoppe|Hoppe]] is associated with covenant communities bound by shared norms. These are pointers to elsewhere in the wiki, not claims this thesis's sources establish. What they share is the attempt to bind liberty to a shared identity; what they lack — on the evidence the wiki actually holds — is any demonstration that such an identity can mobilize at nationalism's scale. The unresolved tension — visible in the sect-ridden character noted above — is whether an *individualist* creed can supply belonging without curdling into the collectivism it opposes. The corpus does not settle it. That a unifying meaning is needed is, on La Boétie's and Arendt's own logic, hard to deny; whether one compatible with liberty can exist is the open frontier.

## Honest Verdict

The reader's critique does not refute the case so much as strip its optimism. The three classic routes are real but individually insufficient against surveillance, propaganda, and the war-ratchet. Stated without flattery, the corpus's defensible position is conditional and narrow:

- **The one hard floor** is the cryptographic cost-asymmetry — the single lever that beats scale and AI — held as a wager, not a guarantee.
- **The one catalyst worth pre-positioning for** is a monetary reckoning, not the war-or-emergency kind of collapse (which ratchets state power) — and only if the hard-money lifeboat is built first.
- **The one missing piece**, which the reader rightly names, is a unifying meaning to rival nationalism's belonging — something the movement has gestured at ([[ayn-rand|Rand]], Bitcoin culture, Hoppe's covenants) but not produced, and may not be able to without betraying itself.

Liberty does not win by out-uniting nationalism on its own ground; it cannot. If it wins, it is by making coercion uneconomic through mathematics, surviving the fiat reckoning with a sound-money alternative already in hand, and — the unproven part — finding a shared meaning that lets free individuals cohere without a master. Human nature is the binding constraint the whole strategy is built around, and the honest answer to the reader is that success is possible but not assured, and depends most on the one thing libertarianism has been worst at: giving people something to belong to.

## Mega-Event Boondoggles: Why Host-City Stadiums Rarely Pay Off — Analysis
URL: /theses/2026-06-12-mega-event-boondoggles
Category: thesis

# Mega-Event Boondoggles: Why Host-City Stadiums Rarely Pay Off — Analysis

> Reuters (11 June 2026): "Instead of building the stadium, they could have built a hospital." Why World Cups and Olympics rarely pay off for host cities — the economics of hosting mega sporting events.
>
> — News post, 2026-06-12

"Why World Cups and Olympics rarely pay off for host cities" reads like a finding about sport. It is a finding about who decides, with whose money, and against what test. Strip the bunting from a host-city stadium and what remains is a capital good commissioned by a political owner who cannot sell it, cannot bequeath it, and will not be holding it when the seats empty — financed by taxpayers who never contracted for it, and judged against its own opening ceremony rather than against the hospital, the bridge, or the private investment the same land, labor, and tax capacity would otherwise have funded. So Reuters reaches the right verdict for almost the right reason. The "rarely" is not bad luck or weak project management; it is the predicted output of a particular property structure and a particular way of deciding. Three lines of argument explain the pattern — and the last shows why the hospital comparison, taken as the fix, concedes too much.

## The owner who keeps no downside

Why would an official reach for an instrument that rarely pays? Because the gain he personally collects and the cost the city eventually carries fall on opposite sides of an election. [[hans-hermann-hoppe|Hoppe]], in [[democracy-the-god-that-failed|Democracy: The God That Failed]], separates two property regimes for the state apparatus. A private owner internalizes the capitalized value of an estate he can sell or bequeath; a public caretaker internalizes only what he can extract before his term ends. [[hoppe-on-caretaker-capital-consumption|Hoppe's caretaker thesis]] states the resulting bias:

> In distinct contrast, the caretaker of a publicly owned government will try to maximize not total government wealth (capital values and current income) but current income (regardless, and at the expense, of capital values).
>
> — [[hans-hermann-hoppe|Hans-Hermann Hoppe]], [[democracy-the-god-that-failed|Democracy: The God That Failed]]

A mega-event is the caretaker's ideal instrument. The opening ceremony, the global broadcast, the construction surge, and the ribbon-cutting all land inside a political term; the maintenance bill, the bond service, and the depreciating concrete arrive after it. The official harvests the current income — prestige, patronage, the photograph — and books none of the capital value he draws down, because he never owned it and could not sell it if he tried. Hoppe states the corollary categorically: "it must be regarded as unavoidable that public government ownership will result in continual capital consumption." The white elephant, on this reading, is not a planning accident outside the model; it is what the project looks like once the coalition has collected the dated, photographed gains and left the amortized, revisable costs to a successor.

[[ludwig-von-mises|Mises]] had already named the policy class this falls under. [[mises-on-capital-consumption|Mises on Capital Consumption]] draws the formulation from [[liberalism|Liberalism]]:

> Antiliberal policy is a policy of capital consumption. It recommends that the present be more abundantly provided for at the expense of the future.
>
> — [[ludwig-von-mises|Ludwig von Mises]], [[liberalism|Liberalism]], Introduction §4 ("The Aim of Liberalism")

What Reuters reports as a stadium that "rarely pays off," Mises would file under a direction of resource flow — from accumulated capital toward present gratification. The "rarely" is structural: it is the output of a policy class whose whole tilt is present-over-future, married to a property structure that rewards precisely that tilt.

## Concentrated glory, dispersed bill

If caretaker incentives explain why officials want mega-events, public choice explains why the polity approves them — why a project that rarely pays survives a vote it should lose on the merits. [[public-choice-and-rational-ignorance|Shughart's public-choice account]] supplies the engine. The benefit — construction contracts, organizing-committee fees, the federation's cut, the favored developer's land — is concentrated on a few who will fight for it; the cost is smeared across millions who barely register a line on a tax bill.

> Small, homogeneous groups with strong communities of interest tend to be more effective suppliers of political pressure and political support (votes, campaign contributions, and the like) than larger groups whose interests are more diffuse.
>
> — [[william-f-shughart-ii|William F. Shughart II]], “Public Choice”

The bid committee, the contractors, the hospitality interests, the bond underwriters, and the officials seeking a national moment are exactly such a group. The taxpayers funding the gap are not — and they have no private incentive to become one:

> Voter ignorance is rational because the cost of gathering information about an upcoming election is high relative to the benefits of voting.
>
> — [[william-f-shughart-ii|William F. Shughart II]], “Public Choice”

This is the boondoggle's life support. The concentrated winners organize, lobby, and log-roll; the dispersed losers will not study a stadium-finance bond before it passes, and the costs are frequently exported to taxpayers in other districts who do not vote on the project at all. Reuters's "Instead of building the stadium, they could have built a hospital" is the dispersed majority's complaint stated *after* the fact — which is exactly the costly attention rational ignorance predicts they will not pay *before* it.

And the cost is not merely diffuse; it is coerced. [[intervention-taxonomy|Rothbard's taxonomy of intervention]] marks the difference. The tax that closes the financing gap is binary intervention — the state takes from residents who never contracted for the stadium; the grants, zoning dispensations, exclusive development rights, and mandated infrastructure clustered around it are triangular interventions that reroute terms the parties would otherwise have set for themselves. The ceremony is voluntary for the spectator who buys a ticket. The financing is not voluntary for the taxpayer, who is the silent counterparty to the whole deal.

## The counterfactual that concedes too much

Having diagnosed the disease, beware the obvious cure. Taken as a remedy, "Instead of building the stadium, they could have built a hospital" keeps the premise that the live choice was between two state projects — that the error was merely picking the wrong one. The objection here is prior to the choice of project. A host-city stadium rarely pays not because planners chose badly but because the means by which it was chosen has no reliable test for whether it picked well at all.

[[political-means-and-economic-means|Oppenheimer's distinction]] marks the line: wealth obtained by production and voluntary exchange — the economic means — versus wealth redirected by coercive appropriation — the political means. The stadium is built with the political means: taxes that redirect existing wealth, not goods produced and sold to willing buyers. That is why "rarely pay off" is structural rather than incidental. A project funded by appropriation and unsaleable afterward throws off no profit-and-loss signal, so — as the [[economic-calculation-problem|economic calculation problem]] holds — there is no non-arbitrary way to know whether the resources were directed to a higher-valued use. Hoppe draws the link in the same caretaker passage: "as public property government resources are unsaleable, and without market prices economic calculation is impossible."

And the missing information is not a spreadsheet city hall failed to fill in. The force of [[knowledge-problem|Hayek's knowledge problem]] is that the knowledge of what each foregone use was worth is dispersed — which parcel would have joined which private plan, which worker would have moved to which job, which neighborhood need would have surfaced first once residents spent their own money. Those facts are discovered through bids, prices, and losses; they are not sitting in a planning office waiting to be compared. A failed stadium does not prove the planner should have known the hospital was optimal. It proves something narrower and more damaging: once the winning project was insulated from capital-market discipline, the process had no way to weigh the real opportunity costs at all.

So the hospital built the same way inherits the same defect. It may be more defensible morally; it is not thereby more calculable economically. Financed by appropriation, held by a caretaker who cannot capitalize its value, and shielded from a profit-and-loss test, it faces the identical caretaker and calculation problems that doomed the stadium's accounting. The reliable cure is not a better choice of state project but the return of the decision to owners who keep the downside and to prices that can be falsified — that is, to the economic means. A stadium is only the most photogenic boondoggle. It rarely pays for the reason no political megaproject reliably does: the people who build it are spending capital they do not own, on a thing they cannot price, for an applause that arrives well before the bill.

## Bitcoin Frees the Individual, Not the Collective
URL: /theses/2026-07-02-bitcoin-frees-the-individual-not-the-collective
Category: thesis

# Bitcoin Frees the Individual, Not the Collective

> Soleimani is right that Bitcoin has dismantled no state and will not — but wrong to conclude it is therefore *not freedom*. He judges a tool of individual exit by the standard of collective liberation, and, finding that it cannot topple regimes, calls the freedom it does deliver an illusion. Held to what it actually promises, Bitcoin buys real if bounded sovereignty for the individual who self-custodies — savings the state cannot inflate away, value it cannot freeze without physically coming for the holder — while doing nothing to break the state's monopoly on violence, which is collective, territorial, and physical. Individual exit and collective resistance are complements, not substitutes. The delusion is not the tool; it is the maximalist promise that a personal escape hatch would free the masses.

## The critique, in its strongest form

In [Bitcoin Is Not Freedom: The Delusion of Digital Escape](https://mises.org/mises-wire/bitcoin-not-freedom-delusion-digital-escape), Hamoon Soleimani argues on Mises Wire that the digital-libertarian faith in a cryptographic exit from the state has been falsified by events. The belief that unbreakable mathematics disarms the state, he writes, "conflates economic friction with true sovereignty." In practice Bitcoin has been "systematically assimilated" — corralled for most users into surveilled, KYC'd custody and Wall Street exchange-traded products — and its most triumphant champions "are now BlackRock, Fidelity, and sovereign wealth funds" — the very concentration of financial power it was built to route around.

His deepest point is about registers of power. Citing Weber's monopoly on the legitimate use of force — "a monopoly that is not economic but kinetic" — he argues that Bitcoin's friction "operates entirely in the economic register" and can never reach "the coercive register where sovereignty actually resides":

> The state has no need to crack a private key; it cracks the person holding it.
>
> — Hamoon Soleimani, “Bitcoin Is Not Freedom: The Delusion of Digital Escape”

The empirical record, he says, confirms it. Iran was not destabilized by cryptography; it commandeered its energy grid to mine what he puts at an estimated 4.5 percent of global hashrate — a figure this corpus's copy of the essay carries undated, so it should not be read as current — and evade sanctions, then imposed an 88-day internet blackout that left dissidents' coins "cryptographically secure but practically useless" — good for nothing with the network severed. Venezuela's Maduro turned the stablecoins millions adopted to survive hyperinflation into "an economic shield for the very regime oppressing them." His verdict: "Cryptographic friction is no substitute for the physical courage required to dismantle authoritarianism." Until its advocates admit it, decentralized networks "will continue to serve as financial instruments for the powerful and political placebos for the desperate."

This is a serious critique, and it is worth stressing that it comes from *inside* the tradition — a Mises Wire piece turning Austrian realism against Austrian techno-optimism, naming the wiki's own sources: [[samuel-edward-konkin-iii|Konkin]]'s [[agorism-and-counter-economics|agorism]], the [[the-sovereign-individual|Sovereign Individual]] thesis of [[james-dale-davidson|Davidson]] and [[william-rees-mogg|Rees-Mogg]], and [[murray-n-rothbard|Rothbard]]'s critique of Konkin.

## Where the critique lands

Much of it lands, and the wiki should absorb it rather than flinch. The custodial and ETF capture is real, and it exposes a premise the triumphalist case usually leaves silent: Bitcoin's freedom is conditional on *self-custody and privacy*, which most users never exercise — a wallet linked to a KYC gateway is, as Soleimani says, an "indelible public blueprint" of a life, not a sanctuary. Regimes do adapt, and worse, capture: Iran and Venezuela show a technology as usable by the oppressor as the oppressed — though Soleimani’s phrase runs the other way round, and is the sharper claim: "autocracies are fundamentally morally agnostic toward technology", integrating whatever fortifies them. And the register argument is correct at its core — the [[political-means-and-economic-means|monopoly on violence]] is physical, and no reallocation of capital into a database negotiates it away.

Most tellingly, Soleimani quotes Rothbard's own critique of Konkin's counter-economics:

> . . .black marketeers might well benefit themselves in the micro sense, but they have no relevance to the “macro” struggle for liberty and against the State.
>
> — [[murray-n-rothbard|Murray Rothbard]], quoted in Soleimani, “Bitcoin Is Not Freedom”

That sentence is the hinge of the whole dispute — and, read carefully, it is where the critique quietly gives the game away.

## The category error: an individual tool judged by a collective standard

Rothbard's line grants the *individual* (micro) benefit as a possibility — "might well benefit" — even as it denies *collective* (macro) relevance. Soleimani inherits both halves but treats only the second as decisive: because Bitcoin does not win the macro struggle, he calls the micro benefit an "illusion of sovereignty sophisticated enough to be mistaken for the real thing." Yet the micro benefit is not a consolation prize; it is the product. Bitcoin's honest promise was never that the state would fall. It was that *you, personally,* could hold value no central bank can debase and no intermediary can freeze without physically coming for you. Judged against that promise, it works.

His own strongest phrase makes the point for him: a private key grants "perfect cryptographic sovereignty and zero political agency." Just so — an individual tool confers individual sovereignty and no political agency, because political agency is a collective achievement the tool never claimed to supply. The Venezuelan who moved savings into a dollar stablecoin got exactly the [[parallel-economy|parallel-economy]] escape from a collapsing currency — Soleimani concedes it was "an organic tool for citizen survival" — even though Maduro later ran state finance over the same rails. Both are true at once. To count the regime's adoption as a *refutation* is to demand that an individual survival tool also topple the government, and then declare it a fraud when it doesn't. It is like judging a lock by whether it abolishes burglary.

## What the tool does reach in the physical register

Soleimani's cleanest overstatement is that Bitcoin operates "entirely in the economic register" and can never touch the kinetic one. The wiki's own material shows otherwise — at the individual scale. In [[softwar|Softwar]], [[jason-lowery|Jason Lowery]] reframes [[proof-of-work|proof of work]] as [[power-projection|physical power projection]] — mainly at national and network scale. Extended to the individual, the same logic implies that *taking* self-custodied coins cannot be done by decree — it needs the holder's key, and so the holder. Soleimani concedes exactly this when he says the state "cracks the person holding it." The concession is narrower than it first looks, and this thesis has already supplied the limit: Iran's 88-day blackout left coins "cryptographically secure but practically useless" without anyone being coerced at all. Denying the *use* of a coin and taking the coin are different operations, and only the second is what proof of work makes expensive. That much still holds: Bitcoin raises the *physical* cost of dispossessing an individual, forcing the state out of the cheap register of the confiscation order and into the expensive one of the rubber hose. It does not seize territory; it makes one person's property costly to take. That is a real, bounded gain in the kinetic register, not none.

The longer-range reply is [[megapolitics|megapolitics]]. The [[the-sovereign-individual|Sovereign Individual]] thesis Soleimani mocks did stake a strong timing claim — Davidson and Rees-Mogg expected the shift to come fast — and events have not borne that out. But the argument that survives the critique is the weaker, long-run one: a gradual drift in the returns to violence, on which today's ETF capture and 88-day blackout are data points, not the final value. Honesty cuts both ways here: the blackout also proves the state *can* still sever the infrastructure at will, which is real evidence for Soleimani and against any near-term escape. The megapolitical claim survives only as a long, unfalsifiable bet — which is a genuine weakness, not a refutation.

## Complements, not substitutes

Strip the maximalism and the two sides converge. Soleimani is right: "Cryptographic friction is no substitute for the physical courage required to dismantle authoritarianism." But the defensible version of the cypherpunk claim never said it was a *substitute*. It said it was a *complement*: individual exit buys time, savings, privacy, and optionality; it can fund and provision the people doing the dangerous collective work; it cannot do that work itself. The error he rightly skewers is the inflation of a personal escape hatch into a theory of mass liberation — the same over-promise the wiki's [[objections-to-libertarianism|objections]] hub and its [[2026-06-08-libertarianism-and-the-adoption-problem|adoption-problem thesis]] already refuse. What remains once it is stripped is not nothing. It is a floor under the individual, not a lever against the state.

## Where it is contested

The synthesis is not a clean win for either side. Four points keep it open:

- **The individual benefit may be thinner than claimed.** If the non-technical majority never self-custody, the freedom belongs to a competent minority, and Soleimani's custodial-capture point bites the median user hard.
- **The megapolitical horizon is close to unfalsifiable.** *It shifts over time* can excuse any present failure; a bet with no settlement date is weak evidence.
- **Exit may strengthen the state, not erode it.** Iran and Venezuela show capture, not withering — the technology fortified the regimes' finances. Individual escape and collective outcome can point in opposite directions.
- **A complement to nothing is a placebo.** Exit is only a complement to a resistance that actually exists; where there is none, Soleimani's charge — that the networks are *political placebos for the desperate* — is exactly right, and the burden falls on the cypherpunk to show that the courage he demands is present, not merely deferred.

The wiki's position is that Bitcoin is real individual sovereignty and no collective salvation, and that saying so plainly is the intellectual honesty Soleimani asks for — arrived at from his own premises.

## The Coordination Objection: A Reply to an Ex-Libertarian
URL: /theses/2026-07-22-dpc-coordination-objection
Category: thesis

# The Coordination Objection: A Reply to an Ex-Libertarian

> The most instructive critique of [[libertarianism|libertarianism]] in this corpus comes not from a hostile outsider but from a developer who knows the arguments, builds the tools, and left anyway. [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|dpc]]'s three objections — that society binds harder than the state, that [[capitalism|capitalism]] optimizes productivity rather than flourishing, and that power can re-consolidate — land partly on ground this corpus already concedes in its own voice. Traced across four years, his trajectory is not a clean exit from the tradition, but neither is it wholly inside it: it moves between libertarian constraints and coercive coordination remedies. His May 2024 remedy for Moloch — a voluntary group whose binding in-group rules work on the halal/kosher model — resembles the unifying meaning that the companion adoption-problem thesis describes as still unbuilt; his coordination-kernel government reads as [[minarchism|minarchism]] only at its narrowest, his 2022 posts giving it a wider, coercive brief. His June 2026 turn toward higher-level holistic economic optimization poses a distinct comparative-institutions question: if higher-level optimization entails economy-wide coercive authority able to override allocation, what makes that concentration sufficiently bounded, contestable, and resistant to capture? His irreducible-power premise does not answer that question, and no surviving post in the cited corpus supplies the institutional comparison.

## The interlocutor

Dawid Ciężarkiewicz, who writes as dpc (@dpc_pw), is a working Rust developer in [[bitcoin|Bitcoin]] and Fedimint — federated [[ecash|ecash]] — infrastructure. He knows the arguments and left anyway, so his departure cannot be answered by introducing him to arguments he already holds: his objection is not that the tradition lacks an account of property, prices, or aggression, but that those accounts do not solve the coordination problems that actually bind individuals. In September 2022 he declared the exit (the spelling in all quotations here is his own):

> I'm an ex-libertarian. I eventually understood and accepted some things: 1) Social and economical pressures are far, far more dangerous and limiting to individual freedom than direct "violence". Humans are social animals and can't survive on their own.
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 12 Sep 2022

The same thread continues:

> Group will always impose its will overpowering the individual. Government is just a formalization of that. You maybe can get rid of government, but you can't get rid of the group. 4) Markets and individual choice are far more stupid and hopeless than what libertarians believe.
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 12 Sep 2022

And, the same day, a self-description:

> Note: I was (and am still strongly leaning) libertarian right ancap.
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 12 Sep 2022

The label coexisted with heterodox positions already in the record: in the months before this post he had endorsed selective protectionism, assigned government a coercive role against coordination failures, once named an unspecified income-inequality intervention among a country's needs, and floated banning or taxing usury. Because those posts predate the self-description, they complicate the label rather than retract it — the weight placed on his stated continuing ancap lean is bounded to an affinity, not a doctrine. No later surviving post in the cited corpus retracts it.

His political posts are a small fraction of a feed otherwise given to Rust, Nix, and Bitcoin engineering, and two limits follow from that. The record is incomplete, since some of what he wrote has been deleted and cannot be read, so the absence of a view is weak evidence. And the posts that remain are the asides of a working engineer, evidence of a trajectory rather than a worked-out program. This reply reads them as a first-person account of exit from anarcho-capitalism by someone fluent in the canon — which is what makes it a rare test case — and holds its conclusions with the modesty owed to a position reconstructed from asides.

## What should be conceded first

Nothing below is argued from a fortress. [[objections-to-libertarianism|Objections to Libertarianism]] names the empirical adoption and stability of a free society among the points where the corpus's answers are weakest. [[criticisms-of-anarcho-capitalism|Criticisms of Anarcho-Capitalism]] rates its own confidence medium, holds [[robert-nozick|Nozick]]'s invisible-hand argument — that a dominant protective agency, and with it a minimal state, would legitimately re-emerge from anarchy — genuinely unresolved, and concedes that no institutional design is self-enforcing: durability rests on culture and ideas more than on formal structure. So when dpc presses on stability, consolidation, and adoption, he is pressing where the tradition, in its honest moments, already gives way. The task of a reply is to establish what his objections do and do not license.

## First claim: society binds harder than the state

*Stated at full strength: a society can respect every formal property title while coordinating so thoroughly against a minority that the minority loses meaningful social and economic agency. If libertarianism calls that society free because no one initiates violence, the [[nonaggression-and-property-rights|non-aggression principle]] guards the wrong perimeter.*

His test case, put to libertarians as a direct question:

> Is a cast system in which super-majority of population forms a socially enforced consensus on treating an arbitrary minority like shit, denying them social and economic opportunities OK with libertarians, as long as NAP is not vilated?
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 12 Sep 2022

The question is built as a reductio, and the honest answer is to bite it. Under [[nonaggression-and-property-rights|nonaggression and property rights]], yes: a caste order enforced purely through shunning, refusal to deal, and social consensus violates no one's rights. The canon's most systematic treatment of exactly this terrain — [[hans-hermann-hoppe|Hoppe]]'s account of [[forced-integration|forced integration]] in [[democracy-the-god-that-failed|Democracy: The God That Failed]] — does not deny the possibility. It treats state-mandated association as the aggression, answers it with voluntary separation, and accepts the illiberal consequence without flinching: covenant communities with entrance requirements, exclusion on whatever criteria their members set. A bullet bitten, not dodged.

Where the objection is strongest is in what the rule measures. [[hannah-arendt|Arendt]]'s distinction in [[on-violence|On Violence]] between [[violence-vs-power|violence and power]] substantially concedes his premise from outside the tradition: power is what people have when they act in concert, and a supermajority's capacity to ruin someone without laying a finger on him is power in the primary sense — the state one formalization of it, which is very close to his own sentence about government. A rule indexed to violence is indexed to the derivative variable, exactly as he says. The concession is about scope, not truth — a rule about when force may be used was never a theory of everything that can go wrong in a human life — but it does make the answer that the NAP is not violated a jurisdictional reply rather than a moral one, and he is right to find it thin.

What the concession does not establish is that a higher sovereign is the cure, and his own words close the escape route: "Government is just a formalization of that." Grant it: then a state empowered to break the caste is the formalization of the very supermajority whose "socially enforced consensus" constitutes it — the group's instrument, not a neutral third party, and so no automatic cure. The NAP guards the violence perimeter not because its theorists judged social pressure harmless, but because that is the one line where the guard does not become the thing guarded against. His anthropological premise, meanwhile, is the tradition's own starting point rather than a discovery deployed against it: [[samuel-pufendorf|Pufendorf]] derives the whole interpersonal law of nature from [[sociality|sociality]] — man too needy to survive without his own kind — and distinguishes imperfect duties of courtesy, whose neglect may be rude or cruel but is not ordinarily compellable, from strict rights. That framework can condemn ordinary refusals without licensing force; it is not a categorical answer to dpc's caste case, because Pufendorf's own treatment of extreme want makes otherwise noncompellable aid claimable when necessary for preservation. Pufendorf himself retains a civil sovereign, so the parallel is to his derivation, not his politics; the real disagreement is the direction of the deduction, from the person's dependence outward or from the group's standing authority down, and the shared premise settles it for neither side.

What remains is the practical question of what erodes a caste consensus, and the tradition's answer is narrower than he wants but not empty: competition, persuasion, exit, the standing cost [[milton-friedman|Friedman]] identifies in [[capitalism-and-freedom|Capitalism and Freedom]] — the man who discriminates pays for it, while rivals have an incentive to hire or serve people he refuses — and the mechanism dpc himself later proposes: intolerant minorities can organize against a caste consensus as well as for one. Whether these instruments are sufficient against a determined supermajority is an empirical question the corpus does not settle. The reply is narrower than a victory: the non-aggression principle remains indispensable as a rule governing enforceable claims and insufficient as a complete theory of social freedom. He is entitled to find that unsatisfying; the question of who enforces the better answer remains either way.

## Second claim: the wrong objective function

*Stated at full strength: market competition is not neutral coordination but a selection process — a cybernetic system that rewards whatever captures revenue and survives, productivity rather than leisure, dignity, or flourishing.*

His earliest formulation predates the exit:

> There's no escaping the fact that capitalism is just a cybernetic system that maximizes productivity growth. Not "humanness", free time, well being or anything else. Only productivity. And productivity is often highly correlated with human well-being. But especially in recent …
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 30 Jul 2022

A continuation of the same thread sharpens what he means by "maximizes":

> And no this is not based on the idea of limited resources. You might be perfectly productive today, but someone more productive shows up tomorrow, and capitalism throws you away as obsolete, not worth maintenance cost anymore. …
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 30 Jul 2022

By 2026 it had compressed into aphorism — "Capitalism is a good servant, but bad master." — and the sharper charge that "capitalism is about the value you can capture, and not the value you create."

Concede the capture point first, because the tradition already makes it at length. The corpus's name for returns that flow to political position rather than production is [[crony-capitalism|crony capitalism]]: [[frederic-bastiat|Bastiat]]'s legal plunder, [[murray-n-rothbard|Rothbard]]'s grants of monopoly privilege, and the [[public-choice-and-rational-ignorance|public-choice]] logic that makes rent-seeking a standing tendency rather than an occasional abuse. The libertarian move is to call this the [[political-means-and-economic-means|political means]] wearing a market mask and therefore not [[capitalism|capitalism]]; he would reply that a distinction unenforceable in practice is not much of a distinction — and a distinction the corpus itself treats as contested. Applied to the Western hybrid that actually exists — the system his February 2026 post describes as "Government overtaken by capital" — his capture line is not an objection to the tradition's account. It is the tradition's account.

The optimizer frame is where the disagreement actually lives. An emergent cybernetic selection process need not contain, or represent anywhere, a global objective function. [[friedrich-a-hayek|Hayek]]'s [[spontaneous-order|spontaneous order]] and the [[knowledge-problem|knowledge problem]] describe coordination among differing ends, not a system consciously optimizing one end. The surviving first post breaks off at "But especially in recent"; its correlation sentence therefore cannot be treated as the last word of the qualification. A later recovered post in the thread sharpens the complaint that can be assessed: firms seek profit and survival, and competition can reward relative productivity while making an otherwise productive worker or firm obsolete. Productivity is one route to revenue and survival, not the sole output selected. Consumer choices help determine what is rewarded; worker choices do too, including choices of leisure that are often made by foregoing income. That does not make markets neutral among all human goods: non-priced values and externalities can be neglected, and exit can be constrained by wealth, dependence, or social power. The categorical only-productivity charge is therefore too strong, but the complaint about outcomes people reasonably reject is not.

The appropriate response need not be either laissez-faire acquiescence or comprehensive planning. Property, liability, associational rules, and other polycentric rule changes can alter incentives and remedy particular harms, though each requires its own account of authority, knowledge, and capture. A higher-level program also faces an aggregation problem when it claims to rank plural ends, but that problem does not show that every correction must abolish markets. By July 2024 the complaint is fully formed and the remedy left explicitly blank: humanity should "organize using tools of cybernetics, distributed systems, complexity theory, game theory, etc. serving our philosophical beliefs and goals." He adds, "Yet there's nothing remotely like that on a political horizon anywhere." In the same post, liberal capitalism was still "the best we can do". His June 2026 post supplies one possible direction, but the comparative question remains which institutions can correct specific failures without creating worse knowledge or capture problems.

## Third claim: power always comes back

*Stated at full strength: every arrangement contains decisions about rules, enforcement, admission, and change. Those decisions create power, and organization can concentrate it. No design abolishes the potential for power or guarantees against consolidation.*

The mature statement came in July 2026:

> "Real anarcho-capitalism have never been tried."
>
> The libertarians have instincts right, but refuse to accept/realize that potential of power is just there, irreducible, and someone sooner or later is going to consolidate it.
>
> Barely ever can have HoA or a chess club without power drama, and somehow we are supposed to have whole societies...
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 15 Jul 2026

It had been building since 2023:

> In practice 99% of the public has no idea what's going on and delegates power to a combination of aristocrats (developers) and oligarchs (businesses). Bitcoin is not exempt from the Iron Law of Oligarchy.
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 30 Jan 2023

This is the objection that lands on the corpus's weakest ground, and the concessions above already grant most of it: his HoA-and-chess-club line is a compressed statement of the stability objection the corpus itself takes most seriously. It is the strongest of his three claims, and it is conceded.

The relevant qualification is that the prospects for consolidation are not fixed across designs. [[megapolitics|Megapolitics]] — the frame of [[the-sovereign-individual|The Sovereign Individual]] — and the [[offense-defense-balance-of-technology|offense–defense balance of technology]] treat the returns to consolidation as a technological variable rather than a constant: when technology creates increasing returns to large-scale violence, coercive organizations tend to grow; when small groups gain cost-effective defensive capacity or returns to large-scale violence fall, power can fragment. That does not repeal the [[iron-law-of-oligarchy|Iron Law of Oligarchy]] or provide a guarantee. It identifies offense–defense and protocol design as relevant variables. The wide historical variation in consolidation is evidence for asking those institutional questions rather than treating all designs as equivalent. This is a wager, not a law. His Bitcoin example gives the institutional comparison a concrete case:

> Personal choice doesn't work collectively. [...] I am freedom loving, but at some point one needs to realize that voluntarily* restricting one's collective short-term freedom is beneficial for one's individual freedom in the long-term.
>
> Bitcoin works precisely because all its users agree to follow restrictive consensus rules. [...] World is full of coordination traps. Unless humans realize they need to navigate these balancing short term and long term, individual and collective, freedom and responsibility, we're doomed.
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 26 Sep 2024

The important word is *voluntarily*. Bitcoin does not eliminate protocol power; it makes rules explicit, verification broadly available, and continued participation conditional on acceptance. As [[21-lessons|21 Lessons]] emphasizes, changing consensus rules requires convincing users to adopt them. [[self-custody|Self-Custody]] raises seizure costs, while [[proof-of-work|proof of work]] raises block-production and history-rewrite costs. His Iron Law post says Bitcoin is not exempt — granted, and this corpus claims exemption for no one. But *not exempt* and *unaffected* are different claims: the design did not abolish the gradient; it changed some costs of climbing it. His own Bitcoin example therefore treats institutional design as consequential. No design abolishes the potential for power or guarantees against consolidation; offense–defense and protocol design can nevertheless affect its scale, scope, contestability, and returns. That is weaker than any promise to eliminate rule and stronger than treating institutional design as irrelevant.

## The convergence: his remedy has the shape of the tradition's open problem

The post on which the convergence rests is from May 2024 — but it was not his first answer to Moloch. In July 2022 the same problem had the opposite solution:

> There is an obvious role for governments and it's keeping Moloch at bay (preventing negative social outcomes of Prisoner's Dilemma). No, free markets can't do it, because it requires coercion. Spare me your libertarian tears.
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 12 Jul 2022

That answer is governmental and explicitly coercive, markets declared incapable and the libertarian objection dismissed in advance. The May 2024 post, in the narrower context of freedom-preserving software, reaches instead for a voluntary group:

> The only solution to Moloh is "religious fundamentalism" like coordination. The reason why software keeps enslaving is that Freedom preserving software can't compete (mostly economically) with larger economy of slave software.
>
> If we were able to create religion like group that one can join to gain benefits, but must respect in group rules, we could win. Think "halal" or "cosher" food, religious fundamentalism. Google Taleb's "the most intolerant win".
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 10 May 2024

The remedy for Moloch — his shorthand for the coordination trap in which freedom-preserving options lose to better-funded unfree ones — is a group joined voluntarily for its benefits, whose in-group rules genuinely bind, propagating on the [[minority-rule|minority rule]] that [[nassim-taleb|Taleb]] names: a compatible product or standard can spread because a strict minority accepts only one option while a flexible majority accepts either, and separate provisioning costs more than offering the common option. That is a design, not a mood. Between the two posts, on his own signature problem, the remedy moved from state coercion to voluntary binding rules — and the later one runs toward the tradition's frontier, not away from it. He never says which it is: whether the 2024 proposal superseded the 2022 governmental remedy, supplemented it, or answered a narrower question about software. No later surviving post in the cited corpus retracts the 2022 position, and the 2024 "only solution" formulation displaces it without acknowledgment — a limit that travels with the claim.

Now set beside it the argument in [[2026-06-08-libertarianism-and-the-adoption-problem|Libertarianism and Human Nature: The Adoption Problem]]: the classic routes to a freer order are each necessary and none sufficient; what mobilizes people is belonging rather than argument; and the missing piece is a still-unbuilt unifying meaning capable of supplying the belonging [[nationalism-and-state-formation|nationalism]] supplies. These are the same shape at different resolutions — his describes the institutional rules, the thesis the belonging that makes people willing to follow them — and his is the more operational: benefits at the door, binding rules inside, an intolerant minority setting the standard. It even has a precedent in the tradition he left: Hoppe's covenant communities, territorial and proprietary where his model is non-territorial observance.

Note the structural symmetry with his own caste case, because it is load-bearing: the halal/kosher device is a socially enforced consensus that binds individuals without violating property — precisely the mechanism his 2022 question presented as libertarianism's embarrassment. The two are not the same object — they differ in purpose, in heredity, in what happens to those outside, and voluntary entry distinguishes the 2024 proposal from a hereditary caste — so the convergence is the narrower, structural point: his proposed group operates in the same institutional space where the tradition locates voluntary association and exclusion, the space [[secession|secession]] and [[seasteading-and-network-states|network states]] occupy in this corpus. The post leaves exit and enforcement unspecified; on the reading that keeps them within voluntary exit and the owner's right to exclude, such in-group rules are associational conditions rather than binding contracts — and under the [[title-transfer-theory-of-contract|title-transfer theory of contract]], which enforces transferred title rather than a bare promise, that is the ordinary right to exclude the [[market-anarchism-and-private-law|private-law order]] is made of. Whether dpc's own group would stay within those bounds, the post does not say. What the post supplies is permission and a sketch, not evidence of an existing institution: it names no group already implementing the design.

His other recurring formulations converge the same way. One puts the coordination function directly:

> What libertarians don't get is that there is an obvious role for "the government", and it's the same as for OS kernel - coordination. The problem with smoking in public places was the "rule of intolerant minority". …
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 11 Sep 2022

A minimal layer legitimated by function resembles [[minarchism|minarchism]] — the night-watchman state argued from systems architecture instead of natural rights. But the metaphor fixes a coordination *function*, not a night-watchman *scope*, and his 2022 posts show he had already filled that scope in with something larger. Two months before the kernel post, the same "obvious role for governments" formula named the role coercively: "keeping Moloch at bay (preventing negative social outcomes of Prisoner's Dilemma)", with markets declared unable to do it "because it requires coercion"; and the same spring he praised the "intelligent use of selective protectionism" of key industries. Minarchism is what the metaphor licenses at minimum, not what he meant — which is why the June 2026 turn reasserts a scope he had shown before rather than inventing one. One month after the exit declaration, he had also already stated the tradition's other answer to consolidation from scratch:

> If you are a Bitcoiner you need to understand: we're all trapped by game theory: we have to support a terrible lying violent gang to protect us from other violent gangs. And having one global gang would be even bigger disaster because it would eliminate the competition
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 16 Oct 2022

That is [[jurisdictional-competition|jurisdictional competition]] in its harshest vocabulary: the answer to irreducible power is not its abolition but its division, so that exit disciplines the price. He will need that argument again below. And his cultural conclusion at the end of 2024 — the ideal human civilization as space-faring Amish, keeping selected technology while refusing what he saw as modernity's self-destructive defaults — is a technologically selective, norm-governed cultural image. It does not by itself establish terms of voluntary entry or exit.

None of this denies his chosen label. Several of his remedies — voluntary rule-bound association, competitive jurisdictions, protocol constraints, a common coordination layer — sit inside the tradition's unresolved institutional frontier; his 2022 posts show others that do not. On the voluntarist half of his thinking he is working on a problem this corpus does not identify the tradition as having solved.

## The holistic optimizer: a comparative-institutions challenge

In June 2026 he supplies a candidate for the higher-level corrector his objective-function critique had implied:

> In The Goal, it's well explained how the cardinal sin of system optimization is optimizing each part in separation. Capitalism is basically each part of the economy optimizing not only in separation but adversarialy to the whole...
>
> In Thermoeconomics in Time of Monsters, it's well explained how Chinese economic model is a combination of bottom level capitalism with higher-level holistic economic system optimization, all contrasted with western economic model.
>
> Quite clear to me that it's a superior way to think about economics, where western squables of naive capitalism with naive socialism now seem like backwater superstitions.
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 26 Jun 2026

The systems insight is sound at the level of an engineered organization: optimizing each component's local metric can degrade a designed whole. The inference to an economy does not follow automatically, because a factory has an owner, a defined output, and a purpose supplied from outside the system, while a society contains people with different purposes and no uncontested scalar measure of the whole.

The Austrian objection has to be scoped honestly. [[ludwig-von-mises|Mises]]'s [[economic-calculation-problem|calculation problem]] is an in-principle result about full socialization: when private ownership, exchange, and money prices for capital goods are abolished, rational economic calculation is impossible rather than merely hard. A market-retaining hybrid keeps capital-goods prices and therefore does not trigger that full impossibility result. It may still distort prices through interventions, and it still faces the knowledge and capture problems; neither point defines the hybrid as not holistic by fiat. Its institutional character depends on what its higher-level authority may direct, override, or leave to market participants. The knowledge problem remains relevant wherever officials substitute their judgments for local knowledge that prices summarize, while any claim to optimize a whole must explain how it ranks plural ends. Neither argument proves anything about a particular economy's growth statistics; both identify trade-offs that an interventionist hybrid must answer.

The damaging objection, though, is not Austrian. It is his own, and he supplies it himself four months earlier:

> As a very pro free markets and personal freedom loving person, I think it is a good time to take an L and acknowledge that just like communism in practice degenerates into totalitarian dystopia, free markets / capitalism degenerates into ... this ... what the West has right now. Government overtaken by capital, masses hypnotized by propaganda, secret societies worshiping Moloch, military industrial complex killing millions, social fabric dismantled.
>
> You might laugh at "real communism have never been tried", and then look at all that is happening and say... "acktually, this is not a real capitalism"? Basically "real capitalism have never been tried"?
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 11 Feb 2026

"Government overtaken by capital" is his capture diagnosis of the Western hybrid he criticizes. His endorsement of the Chinese model names a superior way to think about economics rather than specifying a determinate institution. If higher-level optimization entails economy-wide coercive authority able to override allocation, however, it creates a broad point at which firms may seek political advantage rather than create value. His irreducible-power premise does not demonstrate that such capture will occur or make the endorsement self-contradictory. It makes the comparison of institutions unavoidable: what limits the authority's scope, who can contest its decisions, what countervailing centers remain, and why should its expected capture costs be lower than those of the arrangements it replaces? The cited posts do not answer those questions.

His February post also supplies the discipline that should govern the comparison: he refuses to let capitalism be judged by its brochure — "real capitalism have never been tried" is, on his telling, a laugh line of the same species as its communist twin, and by July 2026 he extends the same mockery to "Real anarcho-capitalism have never been tried." Consistency asks that a proposed higher-level arrangement face the same test. Its case cannot rest on a benevolent description alone; it needs an account of rule change, authority, contestation, and the comparative risk of capture. An April 2024 post identifies the issue directly:

> The question of power still remains: someone has to get to change (or not) the rules.
>
> — [[dawid-ciezarkiewicz|Dawid Ciężarkiewicz]] (@dpc_pw), X post, 11 Apr 2024

If higher-level optimization entails economy-wide coercive authority able to override allocation, that question is especially acute, not decisively settled. No later surviving post in the cited corpus supplies the institutional account. The tension remains an unanswered comparative-institutions challenge.

## The record is not monotonic

A fair reading notes the posts that cut the other way, because the drift is not a straight line. As late as September 2023, a year after the exit, he was still defending capitalism against its lazier critics — the people who never complain about it, he observed, are those who experienced its lack — and in July 2024 he still judged liberal capitalism, for all its flaws, "the best we can do". The competing-gangs post, as libertarian an argument as he has ever made, came one month after the exit declaration; and the 2022 record holds both strands at once — he could write "Sure ideally taxes would be 0%" in the same August 2022 in which he was already weighing whether to "Ban usury altogether" or "Tax usury", weeks after the coercive anti-Moloch post, and two years before the November 2024 post that rejects the libertarian objection directly — its self-description pragmatist rather than convert, its ground basic dignity rather than a rival system, and nothing general about markets following from it.

An August 2025 post puts a third instrument on the same problem the 2024 remedy addressed. Against the prospect of Google and Apple removing Bitcoin apps, and with sideloading noted as itself revocable, he concludes that "the only real and lasting solution is political" — the remedy named being a constitutional amendment guaranteeing freedom of computing. On its visible text that is a limit on power rather than a mandate to coordinate, which would place the remedy inside the tradition rather than outside it. But only the opening of the post survives in readable form, cut off just as it turns to the companies themselves, and an amendment binding private platforms would be a mandate on private property of the kind the tradition refuses — so neither how far he carried the thought nor which way it finally cuts can be read. What is legible is a third answer to the problem, offered a year after the voluntary one.

The pattern across four years is someone holding a market prior and a coordination prior at the same time. That is not confusion but an accurate report of the state of the problem: the 2026 post makes the comparative institutional question more concrete without resolving it.

## What remains contested

Nothing here settles the disagreement, and several pieces of it cannot be settled from this corpus at all.

- **Whether the non-coercive remedies are sufficient.** That competition, persuasion, and exit erode a caste order is a prediction, not a demonstration; voluntary separation shows a NAP-consistent answer exists, not that a society of exclusive covenants would be good to live in. The gap between a rights-answer and a flourishing-answer is the gap his objection names.
- **Whether the state comes back anyway.** Nozick's re-emergence argument is unresolved on its merits; if the stability concession is fatal, it is fatal to minarchism and the holistic optimizer as well — but it is fatal to anarcho-capitalism first.
- **Whether the cost asymmetry holds.** The defense-scaling claim is an admittedly uncertain wager; the [[parallel-economy|parallel-economy]] strategy and [[2026-07-02-bitcoin-frees-the-individual-not-the-collective|Bitcoin Frees the Individual, Not the Collective]] rest on it and are honest that it is a wager.
- **Whether value capture is corrigible.** The standing objection is that the distinction between market profit and political favor is unenforceable in practice; the corpus does not resolve this, and his version of the complaint is the strong one.
- **Whether a voluntary creed can bind without curdling.** A group strong enough to discipline defectors needs a theory of dissent, expulsion, rule change, and exit costs; without one, religion-like coordination can become a socially enforced caste in another form. His halal/kosher proposal and the adoption thesis's creed-and-coordination problem are one question: the cited post names no existing group that answers it, while the companion thesis presents the unifying meaning as unfinished work.

What can be said plainly is narrower. His first and third claims are conceded here in the terms he set them. The second is conceded in its rent-seeking half and answered in its cybernetic half: an emergent selection process need not have a represented global objective, and productivity is not its only route or output. It is not, though, his only departure from libertarian policy: his 2022 posts also hold positions outside any strict anarcho-capitalist or minarchist frontier, coercive government against coordination failures and selective protectionism among them. His trajectory is therefore neither a clean exit nor an orbit wholly inside the tradition; it moves between libertarian constraints and coercive coordination remedies, and the honest description is that motion, not a single fixed position. The frontier the voluntarist half of his thinking works is not whether people need coordination — they do. It is whether coordination can become binding enough to defeat collective-action traps while remaining plural, contestable, and cheap to leave. The sources in this corpus do not show that it can. If higher-level optimization entails economy-wide coercive authority able to override allocation, its advocates must make the comparative institutional case for its limits, knowledge, contestability, and capture resistance; no later surviving post in the cited corpus supplies that case. Whatever he calls himself, on the voluntarist side of his thinking he is working on a problem this corpus does not identify the tradition as having solved.
